ACCEPTThe new classification and the resulting thin-or-one-square coefficient-one theorem are correct under the stated hypotheses. I found no mathematical gap requiring revision. In particular, the chamber reduction survives lateral  $P$  contacts, the bridge incidence argument excludes multiple chambers, and the receiver table remains valid for arbitrary unequal odd tails and feasible exteriors, with the original saturated corrections included.This verdict concerns the written proof in THIN_COMPONENT_CLASSIFICATION_AND_BOUND.md, using the supplied dependencies. It rests on the arguments below; the finite controls and earlier review verdicts are not evidence for accepting this extension.1. Matching-closed chambers with lateral  $P$  contactsThe extension of the pure-rectangle reduction is valid. The essential exterior conditions are indeed conditions on occupancy at the lateral sites.For a matching-closed maximal chamber, every perpendicular occupied neighbor is  $T$ : a perpendicular  $P$  would belong to the same complete endpoint component outside its two supporting rows. Perpendicular selected supports at consecutive columns cannot coexist, because each already has its chamber endpoint as an occupied neighbor.At either lateral end, at most one of the two sites is occupied:Two lateral  $P$ 's would extend the chamber.If one lateral site were  $T$  and the other occupied, that  $T$  would have both its chamber endpoint and the other lateral site as occupied neighbors.Consequently, a doubled corner forces the other corner’s lateral site blank even when its own lateral contact is  $P$ .These facts justify both parts of the construction.Uniform-color case. Promoting the color avoiding all doubled corners removes every opposite-color chamber endpoint. Promoted vertices have no occupied chamber neighbors and at most one exterior occupied neighbor. Whether that neighbor is  $T$  or an unchanged lateral  $P$  makes no difference.Switching case. The guard inequality
$$R_i+L_{i+1}\le 1$$
is correct: the two indicated support sites occupy adjacent positions in the same exterior row. Since the first  $L$  and last  $R$  are zero, the first block with  $R_i=0$  also has  $L_i=0$ .There is one boundary check here that deserves explicit attention. If an existing guard lies at a chamber end, it is the corner opposite that end’s doubled corner. Its lateral site is therefore blank. Thus a zero guard indicator means that the guard has no exterior occupied neighbor, rather than merely no perpendicular support.The HH construction also passes its boundary check. At the left end, the retained row- $q$  endpoint has color  $D$ , so it is the left doubled corner; at the right end it has color  $C$ , so it is the right doubled corner. The central promoted endpoint in the other row therefore has a blank lateral site whenever it lies at a chamber boundary. Its perpendicular support was chosen blank, its horizontal mate is deleted, and its other horizontal neighbor is blank. Its sole occupied neighbor is the retained vertical neighbor.Accordingly, the construction deletes either all  $w$  chamber matching edges or  $w-1$  of them. It is nonempty for every  $w\ge2$ . Original selected vertices remain feasible because the occupied set only shrinks. No additional hypothesis on the lateral contacts is needed.2. The classification and the odd bridge incidence countIsolated full columnsThe width-one exclusion is sound, including configurations with attachments on both sides.With the full column at  $0$  and an attachment at  $(0,-1)$ , the site  $(1,-1)$  is not  $P$ , and its two  $P$  neighbors prevent it from being  $T$ . It is blank. Terminality of  $(0,-1)$  then forces  $(-1,-1)\in T$ , and this support forces  $(-1,0)$  blank.Terminality of the two full-column vertices now forces both
$$(0,1),\qquad (1,1)$$
occupied. Neither can be selected: each is adjacent to its full-column endpoint and to the other occupied right-hand site. Both must therefore be  $P$ , contradicting the isolated full column.The only surviving width-one full column is a component consisting of that column alone, which is the vertical two-endpoint comb. Physical boundaries cause no exception: a required occupied site outside the grid simply makes the proposed configuration impossible.Support alternation and bridge parityA run of single- $P$  columns cannot change rows without disconnecting the component. At either chamber end of a bridge, the absent partner-row site touches two endpoints and is blank. Terminality forces the perpendicular support on the exterior side of the two-row strip.At the next path position, a support on that same side is forbidden by the preceding selected support. Terminality forces the opposite side. This propagates throughout the path and also excludes an additional perpendicular support: at every subsequent position one side is already forced blank.Both bridge ends require the exterior side, so the bridge length is odd. This argument includes a one-vertex bridge. On an outer tail the same alternation holds, and the tip additionally requires its axial selected support.Counting matching exitsFor an odd bridge with  $b$  vertices, let  $e$  be the number of matching edges crossing from the bridge into its neighboring chambers. The remaining  $b-e$  vertices are internally matched, so  $e$  is odd. Since at most one matching edge can leave at each end,
$$0\le e\le2,$$
and therefore  $e=1$ . For a one-vertex bridge, matching disjointness also directly excludes two exits.An outer tail similarly has one exit exactly when its length is odd.A chamber has even order and at most two exits, one at each lateral end. Its exit count is consequently zero or two. Zero would make it matching-closed and contradict the chamber reduction and bundle terminality. Thus every chamber has exactly two exits.If there are  $c\ge1$  chambers and the outer-tail exit indicators are  $e_L,e_R\in\{0,1\}$ , the precise incidence identity is
$$2c=(c-1)+e_L+e_R\le c+1.$$
Each bridge contributes one chamber incidence in total, because it has exactly one crossing matching edge. There is no missing factor of two. It follows that
$$c=1,\qquad e_L=e_R=1.$$
Both outer tails are therefore present and odd.This is an arbitrary-length structural argument, independent of any enumeration.Chamber parity, unique matching, and  $w=2$ Normalize the left tail to row  $0$ . The chamber initially has equally many vertices of each checkerboard color. Removing the two outward-matched corners must preserve that balance, so the removed corners have opposite colors. Hence
$$q+w-1\equiv1\pmod2,
\qquad q\equiv w\pmod2.$$
The residual matching is forced successively: the bottom vertex in column  $0$  must match horizontally to column  $1$ ; the top vertex in column  $1$  must then match horizontally to column  $2$ ; and the alternating argument continues. The odd tails also have their unique matchings after their first vertices are matched into the chamber. Thus the entire matching in the capped case is unique and horizontal.For  $w=2$ , the parity condition puts both tails in row  $0$ . The two lower chamber corners then require selected supports at  $(2,0)$  and  $(2,1)$ . Those supports are adjacent, and each already has its endpoint neighbor, contradicting feasibility. Therefore  $w\ge3$ .With no chamber, connectivity forces a straight horizontal path, whose order is even because the matching covers it. Together with the isolated vertical-edge case, this completes the classification.3. Optional supports and occupied degree fourThe optional-support lists are exhaustive.For even  $w$ , the first tail supports force the north sites at columns  $0,w-1$  blank. The forced south corner supports at columns  $0,w-1$  force the south sites at columns  $1,w-2$  blank. The optional intervals are exactly
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{north: }&1,\ldots,w-2,\\
\text{south: }&2,\ldots,w-3.
\end{aligned}$$
For odd  $w$ , the corresponding intervals are
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{north: }&1,\ldots,w-3,\\
\text{south: }&2,\ldots,w-2.
\end{aligned}$$
There are no additional tail supports: the alternating argument forces the unused perpendicular sites blank, while the axial support forces its adjacent outer sites blank.Every optional selected site already has a chamber endpoint neighbor. Adjacent optional sites in the same row therefore cannot both be selected. Pairing consecutive positions gives
$$k\le
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{w-2}{2}+\dfrac{w-4}{2}=w-3,&w\text{ even},\\[6pt]
2\dfrac{w-3}{2}=w-3,&w\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}$$
The small cases are included:  $w=3$  has no optional positions, while  $w=4$  permits at most one optional support.Alternating selections attain the bound in a completion with the remaining exterior blank. In a fixed feasible exterior, further constraints may restrict which selections are available; that can only reduce  $k$ . The proof does not require inserting every independent selection into every fixed exterior.These supports can raise a chamber endpoint’s occupied degree to four. The manuscript correctly permits that, and neither the freezing argument nor the receiver estimate assumes degree exactly three.4. All odd tail lengths admit an acyclic freezing certificateThe converse freezing claim is valid for unequal odd tail lengths and arbitrary feasible exteriors. Here is an explicit version of the argument, making the dependencies of the two chamber waves clear.Write one tail as
$$p_1,\ldots,p_L,\qquad L\text{ odd},$$
where  $p_1$  is matched to its chamber corner  $p_0$ . Its other matching edges are
$$p_{2a}p_{2a+1}.$$
First freeze the odd-index vertices inward:
$$p_L,p_{L-2},\ldots,p_1.$$
The tip has its perpendicular and axial selected supports. Each subsequent odd-index vertex  $p_j$  has its perpendicular selected support and the distinct permanent neighbor
$$p_{j+1}=m(p_{j+2}).$$
The same construction applies independently to the other tail, whatever its odd length.Both first tail vertices are now frozen. For the left chamber wave, put
$$z_0=(0,-1),\qquad
z_j=(j\bmod2,j-1),\quad 1\le j\le w.$$
The vertex  $z_0$  is already frozen. The vertex  $z_1=(1,0)$  freezes using  $m(z_0)=(0,0)$  and its southern support. For
$$0\le j\le w-2,$$
the vertex  $z_{j+2}$  has the two distinct neighbors
$$m(z_j),\qquad m(z_{j+1}).$$
One incidence is horizontal and the other vertical. This freezes every odd-color chamber endpoint.The opposite-color wave uses the reflected chamber incidences under
$$J(r,c)=
\begin{cases}
(r,w-1-c),&w\text{ even},\\
(1-r,w-1-c),&w\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}$$
Its seed is the already frozen first right-tail vertex. The required chamber matching edges and opposite corner support are reflected correctly.Crucially, this uses reflection only of the chamber and first-tail-site incidences. It does not require reflection of the complete tails, their axial supports, or the exterior configuration. Thus unequal lengths introduce no symmetry assumption.Once the chamber is frozen, freeze each tail’s even-index vertices outward:
$$p_2,p_4,\ldots,p_{L-1}.$$
The first uses its perpendicular support and  $p_1=m(p_0)$ ; each later one uses its perpendicular support and the mate retained by the preceding frozen even-index vertex.These inward, chamber, and outward waves exhaust the component without a cyclic premise. Every witness is an original selected vertex or the mate of an earlier frozen endpoint. The certificate therefore excludes promotions using the component even in global bundles involving other components. Optional supports only strengthen it.5. Arbitrary feasible exteriors and the saturated correctionsThe regional identity
$$\rho(R_H)=T_R+\frac{|H|}{2}-2|R_H|$$
is valid in the scope needed here.First, another endpoint component cannot enter a tile of  $R_H$ . A disconnected nonempty endpoint set in a four-cycle would consist of two opposite corners. Its other two corners could not be selected, since each touches both endpoints. The endpoint belonging to  $H$  would then have at most two occupied neighbors, contradicting its terminality.This observation needs terminality only of the relevant  $H$  endpoint. It therefore also handles feasible exterior completions whose other components have not been normalized.Second, every selected vertex in a receiver tile is adjacent to an endpoint of  $H$  in that tile:With at least two endpoints, their connected subset of the four-cycle is adjacent to every remaining corner.With exactly one endpoint, terminality forces an adjacent in-tile selected vertex. A selected diagonal corner would give that adjacent selected vertex two occupied neighbors.Thus all receiver  $T$ 's occur in the forced or optional support lists. There is no uncounted selected vertex supplied by an arbitrary exterior.Finally, the use of the original charge is justified by matching closure of the whole receiver. Every mate of an endpoint of  $H$  lies in  $H$ , so every saturated-to-deficient transfer incident to the receiver stays inside it. If  $a_H$  is the number of saturated receiver tiles containing an endpoint, then
$$\sum_{\substack{Q\in R_H\\Q\text{ deficient}}}s_Q=a_H.$$
The saturated tiles’ omitted raw excess is  $a_H/2$ , exactly restored by the deficient corrections. Summing therefore gives the displayed regional identity.The all-length count does not discard or assume away saturated attachments.6. Independent derivation of the exact all-phase tableThe table can be derived directly for arbitrary lengths, which also confirms the two-step extension argument.Write
$$L=2a+1,\qquad R=2b+1,\qquad N=a+b,\qquad q=w\bmod2.$$
Then
$$\frac{|H|}{2}=w+N+1.$$
Let  $E$  be the number of axial supports belonging to the receiver. Their membership depends only on the column phase:
$$E=
\begin{cases}
2(1-v),&w\text{ even},\\
1,&w\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}$$
Indeed, the left axial support enters exactly when  $v=0$ , and the right enters exactly when  $v=q$ . Adding two to a tail length preserves these indicators.The chamber rows share a tile band:  $u=0$ The receiver meets precisely the tile columns intersecting
$$[-L,w+R-1].$$
Counting those columns gives
$$|R_H|
=N+\left\lfloor\frac{w+v}{2}\right\rfloor+2-v.$$
The even-position inside supports contribute  $a+b=N$  selected vertices. The axial supports contribute  $E$ . All exterior perpendicular supports, opposite-row corner supports, and optional supports lie outside this tile band. Hence
$$T_R=N+E.$$
Substitution yields
$$\rho(R_H)=-1$$
for both width parities and both column phases.The chamber rows lie in different tile bands:  $u=1$ For even  $w$ , the two bands meet endpoint column intervals
$$[-L,w+R-1],\qquad [0,w-1].$$
For odd  $w$ , they meet
$$[-L,w-1],\qquad [0,w+R-1].$$
For any interval  $[A,B]$ , its number of tile columns is
$$\left\lfloor\frac{B+v}{2}\right\rfloor
-\left\lfloor\frac{A+v}{2}\right\rfloor+1.$$
Applying this to either pair of intervals gives
$$|R_H|=w+2+N.$$
The exterior-side supports at odd tail positions contribute  $N+2$ . Both opposite-row corner supports lie in the receiver, as do all  $k$  optional supports. The axial supports contribute  $E$ . Therefore
$$T_R=N+4+E+k.$$
No even-position inside tail support enters the opposite band’s receiver. The first such left support is at column  $-2$ , whereas that opposite band can overhang the chamber only through column  $-1$ . On the right, the first such support is at column  $w+1$ , beyond the possible chamber overhang through column  $w$ . This remains true for all longer tails and for either value of  $q$ .Consequently,
$$\rho(R_H)=1-w+E+k,$$
which gives exactly the submitted table:Chamber row phaseWidth/column phaseExact  $\rho(R_H)$ Bound from  $k\le w-3$  $u=0$ Any  $w,v$  $-1$  $-1$  $u=1$ Odd  $w$ , either  $v$  $2-w+k$  $\le-1$  $u=1$ Even  $w$ ,  $v=0$  $3-w+k$  $\le0$  $u=1$ Even  $w$ ,  $v=1$  $1-w+k$  $\le-2$ These formulas establish
$$\Delta|R_H|=1,\qquad
\Delta T_R=1,\qquad
\Delta|H|=2$$
whenever either odd tail is extended by two.The manuscript’s geometric explanation is also correct: precisely one new perpendicular support enters the receiver, while the old and new axial membership indicators cancel. Its explicit treatment of this as a comparison of patterns is essential and sufficient. It does not assert a feasible surgery preserving a fixed exterior.7. The neutral  $w=4$  example has its claimed, limited consequenceFor
$$w=4,\quad L=R=1,\quad u=1,\quad v=0,$$
the optional support  $(-1,1)$  is permitted and gives  $k=1$ . The component is feasible and fully frozen by the preceding general arguments, and its full chamber contains three  $P$ -squares.Its counts are
$$(|R_H|,T_R,|H|)=(6,7,10),$$
so
$$\rho(R_H)=7+5-12=0.$$
This remains zero in the original saturated ledger. The two upper end tiles are saturated and have charge zero. Each transfers a half-unit to its adjacent upper chamber tile. With the indicated optional support, those two chamber tiles have original charges
$$+\frac12,\qquad-\frac12.$$
The two lower chamber tiles also have charge zero. Thus the receiver’s total original charge is exactly zero.The example therefore rules out the proposed requirement
$$\rho(R_H)\le-1$$
for every nonstraight frozen thin component. It does not contradict the coefficient-one inequality. It also does not by itself establish equality for the entire ambient grid, because the complementary no- $P$  tiles still contribute their own deficits.8. Union with one-square components under normalizationThe final passage to the initial-pair theorem is valid.Bipartite bundle normalization preserves feasibility and  $|T|+|M|$ , terminates after finitely many matching-edge deletions, and yields full bundle terminality. In particular, the final pair is single-terminal.Every final endpoint component is contained in an initial component. Both alternatives in the initial hypothesis are hereditary under this operation:Containment in two fixed consecutive rows or columns.Containment of at most one all- $P$  unit square.Deletion may split components, but it cannot merge them or create a new endpoint square. Different orientations therefore cause no difficulty.Every final thin receiver has nonpositive charge by the new classification and table, with straight combs contributing zero. Every remaining one-square receiver has nonpositive charge by the supplied one-square theorem. Terminal ownership makes these complete receivers pairwise disjoint, and the no- $P$  tiles form their complement.The exact ledger is consequently
$$\frac{mn}{2}-|T|-|M|
=
\sum_H\bigl(-\rho(R_H)\bigr)
+
\sum_{Q\in Z}(2-t_Q).$$
Every summand is nonnegative. Objective preservation proves
$$\boxed{|T|+|M|\le \frac{mn}{2}}$$
for the original feasible pair in the stated thin-or-one-square class.The equality characterization follows from the same identity, without requiring uniqueness of normalization. For any resulting terminal representative, equality holds exactly when every complete receiver is neutral and every no- $P$  tile has two selected vertices. The new table correctly identifies the sole neutral nonstraight thin case as
$$w\text{ even},\qquad u=1,\qquad v=0,\qquad k=w-3.$$
